# Abstract

This paper tracks the demographic transformation of continental North America (excluding Canada and Greenland) and Bermuda between the outbreak of the Seven Years' War in 1754AD and the Treaty of Paris in 1783AD under CENTAUR-II. Across 26 sub-regional areal masks covering 9.157.164 km² (158.808 five-arcminute cells), total population climbed by 67,4% over twenty-nine years from 2,43M (2.433.616) in 1754AD to 2,66M (2.659.525) in 1760AD, 3,17M (3.171.686) in 1770AD, 3,76M (3.755.094) in 1780AD and 4,07M (4.074.302) at independence in 1783AD [@uscensus1975historical; @wells1975population].

Carving out four emerging frontier and Pacific territories (Kentucky, Watauga-Cumberland in Tennessee, the Republic of Vermont and Spanish Alta California) from the base 1754AD masks captures trans-Appalachian migration and Franciscan mission expansion directly whilst keeping the 1754AD continental sum identical across adjacent chapters [@cook1976population; @greene1932american]. Non-Indigenous inhabitants more than doubled from 1.382.686 in 1754AD to 3.212.352 in 1783AD (including 3.124.922 across the thirteen states plus Vermont, Kentucky and Tennessee), whereas Indigenous nations contracted from 1.050.930 to 861.950 under wartime dislocation, mission epidemics and the 1779-1782AD continental smallpox outbreak [@ubelaker1988north; @cook1976population]. Spatial allocation pairs 93.129 North American site-periods (286.193 horizon site records, regularised $\tau_1 = 1,35$, regularised nugget-to-sill 0,04 with 0 raw nugget across all ten horizons, WLS $R^2 = 0,9990$ to 0,9992) with 1.485 catalogued settlements selected from 1.791 ledger candidates [@paciorek2006spatial; @kelly2025spatiotemporal].

# Background

## Imperial Realignment and Post-1763 Migration

The twenty-nine years from 1754AD to 1783AD bridged imperial struggle over the Ohio Valley and the birth of the American Republic. After the 1763AD Peace of Paris transferred French Canada and eastern Louisiana to Britain and western Louisiana to Spain, British immigration accelerated into Pennsylvania, Virginia, the Carolinas and northern New England despite royal proclamations restraining settlement west of the Appalachian crest [@wells1975population; @greene1932american].

Settler families poured up the Connecticut River valley into the New Hampshire Grants (Vermont) and crossed the Blue Ridge and Cumberland Gap into Kentucky (Harrodsburg, Boonesborough, Lexington and Louisville) and the Watauga-Cumberland valleys of Tennessee [@greene1932american; @forstall1996population]. Simultaneously, Franciscan and presidio expeditions advancing north from Baja California established coastal missions beginning at San Diego (1769AD) and Monterey (1770AD), bringing introduced infectious diseases to dense coastal Chumash, Ohlone and Kumeyaay settlements [@cook1976population; @gerhard1982north].

## Wartime Disruption, Epidemics and Maritime Trade

During the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783AD), British naval blockades, sieges and occupations temporarily hollowed out leading Atlantic seaports. New York fell from 25k on the eve of war in 1775AD to 18k during occupation in 1780AD before recovering to 23,6k at evacuation in 1783AD; Boston fell from 16k to 12k in 1780AD; Newport dropped by half from 11k to 5.532 in 1782AD; and Norfolk plummeted from 6,3k in 1775AD to 1,8k in 1780AD after its 1776AD burning [@bridenbaugh1955cities; @uscensus1975historical].

At the same time, wartime dispersion swelled inland supply towns and temporary army camps across Connecticut and eastern Pennsylvania, exemplified by Litchfield (15.053 in 1775AD), Norwalk (8.837 in 1775AD) and the Continental winter encampment at Valley Forge (11k in 1777AD) [@greene1932american]. Beyond military fronts, vector-borne malaria and port-city febrile outbreaks shaped coastal mortality differentials across Chesapeake, Carolina and Atlantic shipping towns [@bump2022colonialism; @bates2026spatial; @garas2021development], while the 1779-1782AD continental smallpox pandemic struck Great Plains, Plateau and Alaskan Indigenous communities with heavy losses [@ubelaker1988north].

In New England seaports such as Nantucket and Dartmouth, intensive North Atlantic whaling fleets sustained maritime growth into 1775AD before naval warfare interrupted coastal fisheries [@carroll2014intense]. Meanwhile, early naturalists and colonial administrators expanded cartographic and natural-historical documentation across eastern and Gulf provinces, laying the groundwork for post-war federal censuses [@alcantararodriguez2024nature; @forstall1996population].

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Partition and Boundary Continuity

To preserve exact arithmetic continuity with the 1500AD to 1754AD Colonial America module, the 9.157.164 km² domain retains the 22 base polygons whilst partitioning four new frontier and Pacific masks: Kentucky Frontier District (92.734 km²), Watauga and Cumberland Frontier in Tennessee (89.423 km²), the New Hampshire Grants (Republic of Vermont, 26.360 km²) and Spanish Alta California Missions and Presidios (71.637 km²). Adjusting 1754AD baselines across New Hampshire (-300 to 32.100), New York (-450 to 98.923), the Far West (-295k to 290k) and the Trans-Appalachian, Plains and Louisiana-Illinois boundary corridor keeps the 1754AD continental sum identically fixed at 2.433.616 across both modules.

Across 1760AD, 1770AD and 1780AD, all thirteen seaboard states plus Vermont, Kentucky and Tennessee match U.S. Census Bureau Historical Statistics Series Z 1-19 identically [@uscensus1975historical]. Because Series Z ends in 1780AD, the terminal 1783AD benchmark interpolates state-by-state toward the 1790AD First Federal Census reported by Forstall (1996), incorporating Revolutionary War combat casualties and approximately 60k to 80k Loyalist departures to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Québec and British Florida [@forstall1996population; @greene1932american].

Spanish Alta California combines Cook's mission-zone Indigenous series with presidio and pueblo tallies [@cook1976population; @gerhard1982north], while Spanish New Mexico, Texas and Florida incorporate Franciscan and military *padrones* compiled by Gerhard and Jones [@gerhard1982north; @jones1979los]. Long-run biological and secular demographic studies reinforce the importance of separating wartime mortality shocks from underlying high marital fertility across the American mainland [@goldstein2011secular; @pathak2014secular; @hyafil2022evoked; @muzzio2018population].

## Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging and Gazetteer Linkage

Intra-regional spatial allocation draws on the continental North American spatial domain, which integrates 93.129 unique site-periods (286.193 horizon site records) across 3.833 domestic Voronoi catchments (15.517.268 km², or 15,52M km²; 2.570 active inhabited catchments, 67,05% coverage; equivalent circular radius median 29,48 km and 90th percentile 40,95 km overall, 29,3 km and 39,85 km across active catchments; diagnostic Voronoi radius median 29,78 km and 90th percentile 40,69 km; 14,24x over the 6.539 legacy baseline) and 251 cross-frontier conditioning catchments up to 300 km beyond the perimeter across 493.687 valid land cells (18.561.382 km², with 78.938 to 149.138 active inhabited non-wasteland cells across 10 Holocene horizons from 13000BC to 1650AD) [@paciorek2006spatial; @kelly2025spatiotemporal]:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

Following Freeman-Tukey transformation and WLS regression on habitable area, natural productivity, ecozone suitability, fluvial decay and coastal proximity, regularised dimensionless variogram bandwidths sit at $\tau_1 = 1,35$ across all ten horizons (raw 1,519 to 1,6098, mean 1,5782; effective short range 45,23 km to 47,94 km, mean 47,00 km) and $\tau_2 = 2,9025$ (2,9), with raw nugget-to-sill 0 across all ten horizons and regularised nugget-to-sill 0,04 ($\eta = 0,0417$). Urban settlement weights from 1.485 catalogued loci (1.791 ledger candidates; 306 excluded duplicate aliases) anchor provincial port and township gradients before subtracting settled urban cells to conserve rural mask sums [@bridenbaugh1955cities; @greene1932american].

Throughout 1754AD to 1783AD, settled Atlantic and backcountry counties rebuilt from historical county polygons operate under unblurred areal census allocation rather than smoothed pre-contact kriging, keeping provincial and county divides sharp. Across the Trans-Appalachian interior, Great Plains and Far West, unenumerated Indigenous nations retain the 1600AD-anchored Matérn residual substratum stripped of anachronistic twentieth-century Plains cities, coupled with Valley-of-Virginia, Kentucky and Watauga frontier spillover and exact-zero preservation across uninhabited deserts and mountain ranges.

# Testing and Validation

Cross-module checks confirm exact arithmetic continuity at 1754AD (2.433.616 across both the 1500AD to 1754AD and 1754AD to 1783AD Colonial America modules) and exact parity with Series Z 1-19 in 1760AD (1.593.625 across 13 states; 1.595.195 including Vermont, Kentucky and Tennessee), 1770AD (2.121.376 and 2.148.076) and 1780AD (2.677.749 and 2.780.369) [@uscensus1975historical]. Table \ref{tab:validation-1783} presents the benchmark decomposition from 1754AD to 1783AD.

```{r tab-validation, results='asis'}
val_df <- data.frame(
  Year = c("1754AD", "1760AD", "1770AD", "1780AD", "1783AD"),
  Series_Z_13 = c("1.339.906", "1.593.625", "2.121.376", "2.677.749", "2.994.650"),
  Series_Z_16 = c("1.340.406", "1.595.195", "2.148.076", "2.780.369", "3.124.922"),
  All_Colonial = c("1.382.686", "1.643.865", "2.207.026", "2.859.359", "3.212.352"),
  Indigenous = c("1.050.930", "1.015.660", "964.660", "895.735", "861.950"),
  Total = c("2.433.616", "2.659.525", "3.171.686", "3.755.094", "4.074.302"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(val_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  val_df,
  "Reconciliation of Series Z 1-19 state totals (13 states versus 16 including VT, KY and TN), borderlands and Indigenous populations, 1754AD to 1783AD.",
  c("Year", "13 States", "13 + VT/KY/TN", "All Non-Indig.", "Indigenous", "Module Total"),
  list(label = "tab:validation-1783", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

Table \ref{tab:kriging-1783} and Table \ref{tab:kriging-epochs-1783} report variogram diagnostics and WLS covariate slopes across the ten Holocene horizons of the North American spatial domain. Residual $R^2$ ranges from 0,9990 to 0,9992 (mean 0,9991), with raw nugget-to-sill 0 across all ten horizons (0,04 regularised) and active coastal, natural-productivity and ecozone betas guiding rural disaggregation behind the 1.485 colonial towns.

```{r tab-kriging, results='asis'}
na_labels <- c(
  palaeoindian_early_archaic = "1. Palaeoindian & Early Archaic (13000-6000BC)",
  middle_archaic = "2. Middle Archaic (6000-3000BC)",
  late_archaic = "3. Late Archaic (3000-1000BC)",
  early_woodland_formative = "4. Early Woodland & Formative (1000-200BC)",
  middle_woodland_hopewell = "5. Middle Woodland Hopewell (200BC-400AD)",
  late_woodland_dorset = "6. Late Woodland & Dorset (400-800AD)",
  early_mississippian_pueblo_ii = "7. Early Mississippian & Pueblo II (800-1100AD)",
  middle_mississippian_pueblo_iii = "8. Middle Mississippian & Pueblo III (1100-1300AD)",
  late_precontact_thule_oneota = "9. Late Pre-Contact, Oneota & Thule (1300-1500AD)",
  protohistoric_contact_horizon = "10. Protohistoric Contact Horizon (1500-1650AD)"
)
na_horizons <- names(diag_data$variogram_models)
krig_df <- data.frame(
  Horizon = unname(na_labels[na_horizons]),
  Nugget = vapply(na_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$c0_nugget, 6L), character(1)),
  Nugget_Sill = vapply(na_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 2L), character(1)),
  Pseudo_R2 = vapply(na_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$residual_r2, 4L), character(1)),
  Mean_Cell = vapply(na_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$mean_value, 4L), character(1)),
  P99_Cell = vapply(na_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$p99_value, 4L), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(krig_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  krig_df,
  "Continental North American kriging variogram diagnostics across ten Holocene horizons (493.687 valid land cells, 78.938 to 149.138 active cells, regularised tau1 = 1,35, tau2 = 2,9025).",
  c("Kriging Horizon", "Nugget c0", "Nugget-to-Sill", "Residual R2", "Mean Cell", "P99 Cell"),
  list(label = "tab:kriging-1783", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

```{r tab-kriging-epochs, results='asis'}
ep_na_rows <- lapply(geo_data$periods, function(p) {
  pk <- p$period_key
  betas <- diag_data$residual_kriging_wls_betas[[pk]]
  data.frame(
    Horizon = unname(na_labels[[pk]]),
    DomSites = viscount_fmt_number(p$domestic_site_count, 0L),
    BufSites = viscount_fmt_number(p$frontier_site_count, 0L),
    NatBeta = viscount_fmt_number(betas$beta_1_nat, 4L),
    EcoBeta = viscount_fmt_number(betas$beta_2_eco, 4L),
    CoastBeta = viscount_fmt_number(betas$beta_4_coastal, 4L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
ep_na_df <- do.call(rbind, ep_na_rows)
rownames(ep_na_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  ep_na_df,
  "Catchment site-period counts (93.129 unique site-periods and 286.193 horizon site records across 3.833 domestic and 251 buffer catchments) and fitted WLS betas.",
  c("Horizon", "Domestic Sites", "Buffer Sites", "Natural Beta", "Ecozone Beta", "Coastal Beta"),
  list(label = "tab:kriging-epochs-1783", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Results

## Revolutionary Growth Across the Thirteen States (1754 to 1783AD)

Total continental population climbed uninterruptedly from 2,43M in 1754AD to 4,07M in 1783AD despite eight years of warfare (Figure \ref{fig:traj-1783}). Across the thirteen original Atlantic polities alone, non-Indigenous numbers rose by 123,5% from 1.339.906 in 1754AD to 2.994.650 in 1783AD [@uscensus1975historical; @forstall1996population].

Virginia remained the largest state throughout, more than doubling from 275.450 in 1754AD to 447.736 in 1770AD and 601.441 in 1783AD (14,8% of the entire study area). Massachusetts Bay-Maine rose from 202.940 to 365.890, Pennsylvania from 146.581 to 360.025, North Carolina more than tripled from 90.167 to 308.468 as Piedmont farm immigration surged, and Maryland expanded from 149.931 to 267.950 [@uscensus1975historical].

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_colonial_america_to_1783_trajectory.png",
  "Population trajectory across 26 Colonial American, frontier and Indigenous sub-regions from 1754AD to 1783AD.",
  "fig:traj-1783"
)
```

Wartime impacts split sharply between coastal ports and rural hinterlands. Rhode Island suffered an outright provincial contraction during British occupation of Aquidneck Island and Newport, dipping from 58.816 in 1770AD to 53.486 in 1780AD before recovering to 58.230 in 1783AD. New York (rising from 98.923 in 1754AD to 253.315 in 1783AD) and South Carolina (77.530 to 201.502) absorbed port occupations and Loyalist-Patriot civil conflict whilst sustaining backcountry growth, while Georgia jumped sixfold from 10.951 to 66.414 [@wells1975population; @uscensus1975historical].

## Trans-Appalachian Frontiers, Borderlands and Indigenous Nations

West of the crest and north into the New Hampshire Grants, frontier settlement grew explosively between 1760AD and 1783AD (Table \ref{tab:regions-1783}, Figure \ref{fig:shares-1783}). Vermont climbed from 750 inhabitants in 1754AD and 1.420 in 1760AD to 10.180 in 1770AD, 47.770 in 1780AD and 59.102 at 1783AD across 174 catalogued townships led by Bennington (1,85k) and Guilford (1.683).

Kentucky jumped from 2,5k in 1754AD to 17,2k in 1770AD and 54.453 in 1783AD as stockaded stations along the Kentucky and Ohio rivers expanded rapidly, while Watauga-Cumberland in Tennessee rose from 6k to 21.557 [@greene1932american; @forstall1996population]. Together, Kentucky, Tennessee and Vermont added 135.112 residents by 1783AD.

```{r fig-shares, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_colonial_america_to_1783_shares.png",
  "Shift in demographic shares from interior Indigenous territories toward Atlantic and trans-Appalachian polities, 1754AD to 1783AD.",
  "fig:shares-1783"
)
```

```{r tab-regions, results='asis'}
yr_cols <- c("1754", "1760", "1770", "1780", "1783")
reg_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[[y]]), character(1))
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  nm <- gsub("\\s*/\\s*", " and ", nm, perl = TRUE)
  nm <- sub("\\s*\\(Cherokee.*\\)$", "", nm)
  df_r <- data.frame(
    Region = nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
    df_r[[yr_cols[idx]]] <- vals[idx]
  }
  df_r
})
reg_df <- do.call(rbind, reg_rows)
tot_vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[y]]), character(1))
tot_row <- data.frame(
  Region = "Module Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$total_area_km2, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
  tot_row[[yr_cols[idx]]] <- tot_vals[idx]
}
reg_df <- rbind(reg_df, tot_row)
rownames(reg_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  reg_df,
  "Sub-regional population totals across 26 territories of North America, 1754AD to 1783AD.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area (km²)", "1754AD", "1760AD", "1770AD", "1780AD", "1783AD"),
  list(label = "tab:regions-1783", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 28L)
)
```

Conversely, Indigenous and mission-frontier populations declined across every western zone. The 1779-1782AD smallpox pandemic and frontier warfare cut the Great Plains from 192k in 1754AD to 148,25k in 1783AD (-22,8%), the Far West from 290k to 260k (-10,3%), Trans-Appalachian confederacies from 81,2k to 71k (-12,6%) and Alaska-Aleutians from 64.180 to 49.950 (-22,2%) [@ubelaker1988north].

In Spanish Alta California, the establishment of eleven Franciscan missions and presidios between 1769AD and 1782AD accelerated coastal Indigenous mortality, reducing total regional population from 295k in 1754AD to 252,68k in 1783AD [@cook1976population]. Across the Spanish Gulf-Southwest borderlands, Florida briefly swelled to 8,1k in 1780AD under Loyalist wartime refugees at St. Augustine before easing to 7,6k in 1783AD, New Mexico rose gently from 47,4k to 51,8k, Texas eased from 17,9k to 15.650 and Louisiana-Illinois recovered from 59,5k in 1770AD to 65,5k in 1783AD as Acadian exiles and river traders reinforced New Orleans (4,8k) and St. Louis [@gerhard1982north; @jones1979los].

## Regional Density and Urban Concentration

Table \ref{tab:density-1783} tracks settlement coverage (1.485 included loci) and areal density shifts across all 26 territories. By 1783AD, coastal New England and the Chesapeake had crossed 14 to 22 persons per km² (Rhode Island reaching 22,45 persons per km², Connecticut 17,59, Maryland 14,68, Pennsylvania 12,16 and Delaware 8,94, while Bermuda held 190,57 persons per km²), whereas vast interior plains and boreal Alaska remained at or below 0,06 persons per km².

```{r tab-density-1783, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
dens_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  ar <- as.numeric(rv$area_km2)
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  nm <- gsub("\\s*/\\s*", " and ", nm, perl = TRUE)
  nm <- sub("\\s*\\(Cherokee.*\\)$", "", nm)
  n_sites <- sum(vapply(sett_data, function(s) identical(s$region_id, rk), logical(1)))
  p54 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1754"]])
  p83 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1783"]])
  chg <- 100 * (p83 - p54) / p54
  data.frame(
    Region = nm,
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    D54 = viscount_fmt_number(p54 / ar, 2L),
    D83 = viscount_fmt_number(p83 / ar, 2L),
    Change = paste0(ifelse(chg >= 0, "+", ""), viscount_fmt_number(chg, 1L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
dens_df <- do.call(rbind, dens_rows)
rownames(dens_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  dens_df,
  "Catalogued settlements (total 1.485), 1754AD and 1783AD areal densities (persons per km²) and percentage population change across all 26 masks.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Sites", "1754AD (km²)", "1783AD (km²)", "Change"),
  list(label = "tab:density-1783", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 28L)
)
```

Urban rank-size hierarchy also restructured markedly across the war years. Philadelphia climbed to 36k in 1783AD (flanked by its northern suburbs No. Liberties at 8,3k and Northern Liberties at 7,8k), outpacing war-occupied New York (23,6k in 1783AD; 25k in 1775AD) and Boston (16k), while Baltimore surged nineteenfold from 500 in 1754AD to 9,5k in 1783AD as Chesapeake grain exports eclipsed tobacco [@bridenbaugh1955cities; @forstall1996population].

## Sub-Regional Profiles and Frontier Carve-Outs

To trace how trans-Appalachian and Pacific frontiers separated from colonial seaboard provinces and Indigenous homelands without altering continental 1754AD sums, Table \ref{tab:frontier-transitions-1783} isolates the four newly delineated territories alongside their five bordering parent masks across all five benchmark years.

```{r tab-frontier-transitions, results='asis'}
trans_keys <- c(
  "ca2_vermont_republic",
  "ca1_new_hampshire",
  "ca1_new_york",
  "ca2_kentucky_frontier",
  "ca2_watauga_cumberland_frontier",
  "ca1_virginia",
  "ca1_north_carolina",
  "ca2_alta_california_missions",
  "ca1_far_west_indigenous_1754"
)
trans_rows <- lapply(trans_keys, function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  nm <- gsub("\\s*/\\s*", " and ", nm, perl = TRUE)
  nm <- sub("\\s*\\(.*$", "", nm)
  data.frame(
    Mask = nm,
    Y54 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(rv$population[["1754"]]), 0L),
    Y60 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(rv$population[["1760"]]), 0L),
    Y70 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(rv$population[["1770"]]), 0L),
    Y80 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(rv$population[["1780"]]), 0L),
    Y83 = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(rv$population[["1783"]]), 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
trans_df <- do.call(rbind, trans_rows)
rownames(trans_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  trans_df,
  "Benchmark series across the four newly delineated frontier and Pacific masks alongside adjacent parent territories, 1754AD to 1783AD.",
  c("Sub-Region", "1754AD", "1760AD", "1770AD", "1780AD", "1783AD"),
  list(label = "tab:frontier-transitions-1783", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

### New England and the Republic of Vermont

Across the five northern masks covering 164.803 km², total population doubled from 399.190 in 1754AD to 803.898 in 1783AD (+101,4%), rising faster in inland hill towns and northern valleys than on crowded maritime peninsulas [@uscensus1975historical; @forstall1996population]. Massachusetts Bay (including District of Maine) grew from 202.940 to 365.890, anchored by Boston (16k), Salem and rural Maine timber ports, while New Hampshire expanded more than threefold from 32.100 to 104.129. Connecticut reached 216.547 (17,59 persons per km²), led by interior Litchfield (15.053), coastal Norwalk (8.837) and New Haven (8.295), whereas exposed Rhode Island dropped between 1770AD (58.816) and 1780AD (53.486) during the British occupation of Newport before recovering to 58.230 in 1783AD [@greene1932american; @bridenbaugh1955cities]. Meanwhile, settled farming townships poured across the Green Mountains into the Republic of Vermont, lifting that 26.360 km² mask nearly eightyfold from 750 in 1754AD to 59.102 in 1783AD around Bennington (1,85k) and Guilford (1.683) [@uscensus1975historical].

### Mid-Atlantic Provinces and Wartime Supply Corridors

The four Mid-Atlantic provinces covering 90.904 km² expanded by 128,6% from 356.917 in 1754AD to 816.089 in 1783AD, absorbing heavy Scots-Irish, Palatine German and English migration before the outbreak of fighting in 1775AD [@wells1975population; @uscensus1975historical]. Pennsylvania surged from 146.581 to 360.025, sustaining both the continent's largest port complex at Philadelphia (36k) flanked by No. Liberties (8,3k) and Northern Liberties (7,8k) and major military logistics nodes such as Valley Forge (11k during the 1777AD winter encampment), Lancaster and York [@bridenbaugh1955cities; @greene1932american]. New York climbed from 98.923 to 253.315 even with lower Manhattan occupied until November 1783AD, while New Jersey (80.761 to 153.181) and Delaware (30.652 to 49.568) experienced alternating Continental and Crown troop quartering along the Hudson-Delaware plain.

### Chesapeake, Carolinas, Georgia and Bermuda

Together, the five southern states and Bermuda spanned 371.899 km² and increased by 137,1% from 613.929 in 1754AD to 1.455.875 in 1783AD, propelled by piedmont backcountry farmstead clearance and enslaved African labour importation across tidewater and rice-coast estates [@uscensus1975historical; @bump2022colonialism]. Virginia remained the most populous American territory throughout, climbing from 275.450 in 1754AD to 601.441 in 1783AD despite wartime raids along the James River, while North Carolina (90.167 to 308.468) and South Carolina (77.530 to 201.502, anchored by Charleston at 12,5k) filled their piedmont counties rapidly after the Seven Years' War. Georgia registered the steepest percentage growth among coastal states, rising more than sixfold from 10.951 to 66.414, whereas island Bermuda stabilised near resource carrying capacity at 10.100 (190,57 persons per km²) [@wells1975population].

### Kentucky and Watauga-Cumberland Frontiers

West of the Appalachian divide, Virginia and North Carolina militia families pushed through Cumberland Gap and down the Holston Valley into the Kentucky Frontier District (92.734 km²) and Watauga-Cumberland Settlements (89.423 km²), lifting combined mask population by 794,2% from 8.500 in 1754AD to 76.010 in 1783AD [@greene1932american; @uscensus1975historical]. Kentucky dipped modestly during the Seven Years' War to 2.350 in 1760AD before accelerating to 17.200 in 1770AD, 46.000 in 1780AD and 54.453 in 1783AD across fortified stations at Harrodsburg (750), Lexington (600), Louisville (550), Boonesborough (400) and Shawnee trading towns such as Lower Shawneetown (1,1k). Across Tennessee, Overhill Cherokee towns including Chota (850) and Great Tellico (680) coexisted tensely with emerging Cumberland stations around Fort Nashborough (450), raising the Watauga-Cumberland total from 6.000 to 21.557 by 1783AD.

### Spanish Borderlands, Alta California and Interior Indigenous Nations

Across the five Spanish and former French territories covering 1.590.194 km², total population eased by 8,1% from 427.700 in 1754AD to 393.230 in 1783AD as coastal Alta California losses outweighed steady Hispanic town growth elsewhere [@cook1976population; @gerhard1982north; @jones1979los]. Spanish Alta California (71.637 km²) contracted from 295.000 in 1754AD to 252.680 in 1783AD as neophyte epidemics spread around San Diego (850), San Gabriel (750), Monterey and Santa Clara while Yokuts villages near Tulare Lake (1,75k) remained outside mission control [@cook1976population]. Conversely, Spanish New Mexico recovered slowly from 47.400 to 51.800, French-Spanish Louisiana and Illinois rebounded after 1770AD (59.500) to 65.500 in 1783AD around New Orleans and St. Louis, Spanish Florida grew from 6.100 to 7.600 following diplomatic retrocession, and Spanish Texas slipped from 17.900 to 15.650. Meanwhile, the four predominantly Indigenous interior regions covering 6.757.207 km² declined by 15,6% from 627.380 in 1754AD to 529.200 in 1783AD (Trans-Appalachian 81.200 to 71.000, Great Plains 192.000 to 148.250, Far West 290.000 to 260.000, and Alaska 64.180 to 49.950), with the sharpest mortality occurring during the 1779-1782AD smallpox epidemic [@ubelaker1988north; @milner2010].

## Archaeological Source Structure behind the Continental Raster

To contextualise the rural spatial weights behind these 26 masks, Table \ref{tab:source-corpora-1783} summarises the constituent archaeological and gazetteer source corpora feeding the 93.129 continental site-periods (286.193 horizon site records) of the North American spatial domain [@kelly2025spatiotemporal; @milner2010; @paciorek2006spatial].

```{r tab-source-corpora, results='asis'}
sc <- geo_data$source_counts
sc_names <- c(
  KellyRobinson_L48 = "Kelly and Robinson (Lower 48 Radiocarbon)",
  CENTAUR_Gazetteer = "CENTAUR Settlement Gazetteer Anchors",
  Greenland_Nunniffiit = "Greenland Nunniffiit Coastal Sites",
  c14_cleaned_dedup = "Canadian and Boreal Radiocarbon (Deduplicated)",
  SWSN_CriticalScales = "Southwest Social Networks Critical Scales",
  p3k14c_2025 = "p3k14c North America Subset",
  VEP_MesaVerde = "Village Ecodynamics Project (Mesa Verde)",
  Texas_RCD3 = "Texas Archaeological Radiocarbon Database",
  CENTAUR_Colonial = "CENTAUR Colonial Parish and Frontier Corpus",
  Milner2023 = "Eastern Woodland Mississippian Centres",
  NPS_NRHP_Arch = "NPS National Register Indigenous Monuments",
  KohlerReese_NDT = "Kohler and Reese Neolithic Demographic Series",
  Plains_Earthlodges = "Plains Village Earthlodge Compendium",
  POLARIS_Chukotka = "Beringian and Chukotka Perimeter Anchors"
)
sc_keys <- names(sc_names)
sc_vals <- vapply(sc_keys, function(k) as.numeric(sc[[k]]), numeric(1))
sc_tot <- sum(sc_vals)
sc_df <- data.frame(
  Corpus = unname(sc_names),
  SitePeriods = vapply(sc_vals, function(v) viscount_fmt_number(v, 0L), character(1)),
  Share = paste0(vapply(100 * sc_vals / sc_tot, function(v) viscount_fmt_number(v, 2L), character(1)), "%"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(sc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sc_df,
  "Constituent continental site-period corpora pooled into the non-stationary Matérn kriging prior (Northern America spatial domain).",
  c("Source Corpus", "Site-Periods", "Share"),
  list(label = "tab:source-corpora-1783", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Limitations

Four limitations govern the 1754AD to 1783AD reconstruction. First, Revolutionary War displacement, combining military deaths, prisoner-ship losses and roughly 60k to 80k Loyalist departures to British North America, Nova Scotia and the Caribbean, introduces roughly +/- 8% uncertainty around the 1783AD intercensal bridge between Series Z 1780AD figures and the 1790AD First Federal Census [@forstall1996population; @wells1975population; @greene1932american]. Second, British port occupations disrupted local tax lists and Anglican parish burials in New York, Newport, Savannah and Charleston between 1776AD and 1782AD, requiring interpolation across irregular muster and evacuation returns [@bridenbaugh1955cities].

Third, the 1779-1782AD smallpox epidemic across the Great Plains, Columbia Plateau and Alaska lacks continuous ecclesiastical registers, forcing mortality trajectories to rely on Hudson's Bay Company and St. Louis fur-trade journals alongside ethnohistorical mortality multipliers that carry +/- 26% to +/- 38% confidence bounds [@ubelaker1988north].

Fourth, western land claims of Virginia, North Carolina and Georgia in 1783AD remained overlapping until post-war federal cessions. Partitioning fixed 1783AD masks for Kentucky and Watauga-Cumberland isolates trans-Appalachian frontier growth cleanly without double counting parent tidewater state populations, handing off identically to post-independence United States modules at 1783AD [@forstall1996population].

# Conclusion

Between 1754AD and 1783AD, continental North America south of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence line experienced rapid settler expansion paired with sharp wartime port shocks and western Indigenous decline. Total regional population increased by 67,4% from 2,43M to 4,07M, while the non-Indigenous share rose from 56,8% to 78,8%, crossing the Appalachians into Vermont (59.102), Kentucky (54.453) and Watauga-Cumberland (21.557) as Spanish missions advanced along coastal California (252.680). Anchored identically at 1754AD (2.433.616) and 1783AD (4.074.302) across twenty-six sub-regional masks, 93.129 continental site-periods (286.193 horizon site records, regularised $\tau_1 = 1,35$, $\tau_2 = 2,9025$, effective short range 45,23 km to 47,94 km, mean 47,00 km) and 1.485 catalogued settlements from 1.791 ledger candidates, this module links colonial provincial registers directly to the federal census era.
